introduction: The guide lays its condition down at once: whoever arises to teach must first be adorned with an upright character, and must deliver the Cause to himself before he delivers it to anyone else. The readings then describe the teacher they have in mind, pure in intention, detached, sure of help and not of his own ability, learned and yet willing to be silent, gentle, humble, tireless, and careful about when and to whom he speaks. It is a portrait drawn many times before. Chaucer’s parson did first and taught afterwards; Paul feared being a castaway after preaching to others; the Dhammapada and the Qur’an both tell the teacher to begin with himself; Confucius waits for the eager pupil, and Moses asks for a knot to be loosed from his tongue. The portrait has also been questioned, and those questions are here. Paul rejoices that Christ is preached even from envy. Mencius suspects the wish to teach. Milton finds a service in waiting, and the Gospel tells tired disciples to rest. The lost sheep is sought when the readings say to turn away, the apostles obey God rather than men, and Confucius counts it knowledge to admit what one does not know. Together they ask how anyone becomes fit to teach, and whether fitness can be waited for.
questions: The teacher must first teach himself. Portia says how hard that is, and Mencius doubts the motive. If character must come before teaching, who may begin, and when?
“The intention of the teacher must be pure.” Paul rejoiced that Christ was preached “whether in pretence, or in truth”. Does the worth of what is taught depend on the one who teaches it?

The readings tell a speaker not to look to his own ability but to turn, ask and speak. What do Aesop’s waggoner, Pope’s “little learning” and Confucius on knowing what one does not know add to that advice?
“If thou findest one who turneth away, turn from him.” Read this with the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine, and with the dust shaken from the feet. How does a teacher know which is called for?

Several readings counsel caution, toward rulers, toward newcomers and about speaking openly. Others ask for courage and unceasing effort. How do the housetops, “obey God rather than men”, and “entertain strangers” help in weighing the two?

“Rest not for a moment”, the readings say; “rest a while”, says the Gospel, and Milton finds that those also serve who wait. What would a sustainable life of service look like in the light of all three?

outside.why: Whoever teaches “must needs, ere he proclaimeth His Message, adorn himself with … an upright and praiseworthy character”. Chaucer’s parson is remembered for that order: first he did, and afterwards he taught.

Character must come before proclamation, the reading says. Portia admits what that asks: it is easier to teach twenty what is good than to be one of the twenty who follow one’s own teaching. Who, on the reading’s terms, would ever be ready to begin?
“Teaching the cause of God is not only through the tongue; it is through deeds, a good disposition, happiness.” Whitman says of himself and his companions that they convince by presence.

“The intention of the teacher must be pure.” Paul knew preachers whose intention was envy and strife, and rejoiced all the same, because Christ was preached. Does a message depend on the motive of the one who carries it?

The reading lists what a teacher’s heart must be: pure, independent, at peace. Mencius names what it usually is: people like to be teachers of others. How would a teacher know which of the two is moving him?
One who would deliver the Cause must “first … deliver it unto himself, then unto the people”. The Dhammapada gives the same sequence: direct yourself first, then teach others.
Without teaching himself first, the reading says, a teacher’s words “will never influence the hearts”. The Qur’an asks those who enjoin righteousness and forget themselves whether they have no sense.
The Message is delivered “only through goodly deeds and spiritual attributes”, and then clear utterance. Confucius on the superior man: he acts before he speaks.

The friends are to guard their dignity so “that all nations shall come to know and honour them for their trustworthiness”. The Gospel warns against goodness done to be seen. What is the difference between being known for integrity and seeking to be?

“An eloquent preacher, like the bearer of Joseph’s shirt, may himself be unaware and deprived of its sweet fragrance.” Paul feared it for himself: that having preached to others, he should be a castaway.
“May we not speak before hearing.” The Letter of James makes it a rule for everyone: swift to hear, slow to speak.
The reading prays not to speak before hearing nor command before being commanded. Laozi observes that the one who knows is not eager to speak.
“Today pure words and sincere deeds are beloved”; nothing else is accepted. The First Letter of John asks for love in deed and in truth, not in word.
Whoever has recognized God must “quicken dead souls” by the breath of the All-Merciful. Ezekiel prophesies to the breath over a valley of the slain, and they live.
“Be thou of such character that the sincere ones may find from thee the fragrances of the All-Merciful.” Paul: we are a sweet savour of Christ in every place.

“Be not, like children, occupied with diverse colors nor take delight therein.” Keats holds that a thing of beauty is a joy for ever and that its loveliness binds us rightly to the earth. Is delight in colours always childish?
The reading asks “a whole-hearted surrender of our will to the Will of God”. The pattern of such surrender is Gethsemane: not as I will, but as thou wilt.

“A complete self-surrender” is the reading’s requirement. Polonius’s is the reverse: this above all, to thine own self be true. Which self is surrendered, and which must a teacher keep in order to be honest with his hearers?

Teachers are to “be satisfied with little food”. The Preacher counts it good and comely to eat and drink and enjoy the fruit of one’s labour, as a gift of God. How much austerity does the work require, and when does it become a display?
God will inspire whoever is detached, “and will cause the pure waters of wisdom and utterance to gush out”. The Gospel promises that what to say will be given in that hour.
“Today is the day for service and rising up, not for sitting down and dreaming idle dreams.” Longfellow: not enjoyment and not sorrow, but to act.

The reading has no place for sitting still. Milton, blind in middle life, heard Patience tell him that God needs no one’s work, and that they also serve who only stand and wait. Is there a service that looks like sitting down?
“If thoughts of life do linger in thy heart, approach not here; but if thy soul thou wouldst surrender, bring it and more.” The Gospel: whoever will save his life shall lose it.
“If not equipped for this path, burden us not, withdraw.” Jesus tells would-be followers to count the cost first, like a man about to build a tower.

The verse asks for a life surrendered or nothing. Falstaff, who lives by the opposite rule, has given it its motto: the better part of valour is discretion. Is there a prudence that is not Falstaff’s, and where do these readings allow it?
The servant of the Cause is one who could “pass by cities of gold and silver” without opening his eyes. Jesus is shown all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and answers in a sentence.
“Take no rest by day nor repose by night.” The charge to Timothy: be instant in season, out of season.

What is asked is “detachment from all that hath been seen and heard, and thereafter to observe and hearken with the eye and ear of truth and fairness”. Bacon made that clearing of the mind the first step of science: the understanding is no dry light, and believes what it would like to be true.

The reading wants a hearer detached from everything previously seen and heard. Pascal thought the heart has reasons that reason does not know. Can a person, or should a person, set aside everything he has loved in order to judge fairly?
“The mirrors of your hearts ye must purify, and your vision ye must rectify.” The Beatitude joins the same two: the pure in heart shall see.
“Rest you assured that the breathings of the Holy Spirit will loosen your tongue.” Moses, slow of speech, is told: I will be with thy mouth.
Before speaking, the reading says, turn and ask for confirmation. Moses’ prayer in the Qur’an is the model: ease my task, and loose a knot from my tongue.
“Good deeds alone, without the recognition of God, cannot lead to eternal redemption.” The Letter to the Ephesians: by grace, through faith, not of works.

The reading denies that good deeds suffice without recognition. Pope says in a couplet what many have felt against that: his can’t be wrong whose life is in the right. What does the reading think the good life lacks?
“Do thou not behold thine own capability and ability.” Paul was told that strength is made perfect in weakness.

The reading tells the teacher to look away from his own ability and ask for help. Aesop’s Hercules tells the waggoner to stop asking and use his shoulder. How much of a speaker’s preparation is prayer, and how much work?
“Carrying in your hands the swords of light, ye may conquer the kingdoms of the hearts.” The Letter to the Ephesians has the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

“Be not like the heedless … who would first lament from the pulpit the oppression” of the holy ones, and then curse and condemn their Chief. Jesus says the same of those who adorn the tombs of the prophets their fathers killed.
Be “so aflame, that your holy melodies” rise to the Concourse on high. Jeremiah’s word was a fire shut up in his bones.

“Arise … with a genuine zeal and ardour and with a flame.” Paul, who had been zealous on the wrong side, bears his former companions witness that they have zeal, “but not according to knowledge”. What keeps ardour honest?
“God has created in thee a great capability. Thou must expend this capability in the Cause of the Kingdom.” The parable of the talents praises the servant who put his five to work.
“Do not look upon thyself and thine own capacity.” The treasure, says Paul, is in earthen vessels, so that the power may be seen to be God’s.
“Engage in guiding souls and strive to acquire divine sciences and arts.” Tennyson: let knowledge grow from more to more, but more of reverence in us dwell.
The teacher is to acquire sciences and arts. Pope warns that a little learning is the dangerous amount. How much should someone know before presuming to guide another?
“Capacity is needed. Pure soil is required for the rain of mercy to bring forth flowers.” The sower’s seed is the same everywhere; the ground differs.
When people “ask difficult questions”, turn, ask assistance, and speak with courage. The First Letter of Peter: be ready always to give an answer, with meekness and fear.

The reading promises that the Holy Spirit will confirm a speaker faced with hard questions. Confucius defines knowledge as holding that you know what you know and allowing that you do not know what you do not. What should a teacher say when the honest answer is “I do not know”?
“As hearing ears are scarce to find … silence hath taken precedence over utterance.” The Preacher: a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
“O high priests! Ears have been given you that they may hearken.” Jesus addresses the religious learned of his day more harshly: they shut the kingdom, neither entering nor letting others enter.

The reading asks for “fluent speakers” who are detached and purified. Paul came to Corinth in weakness and trembling and without enticing words, so that faith should not rest on a speaker’s skill. How much should fluency count?
“Bear not witness to that which thou hast not attained.” Jesus tells Nicodemus: we speak that we do know, and testify that we have seen.
True educators “will first arouse and stir their capacities before offering any bounty”. Confucius would not open the truth to one who was not eager, and waited for the other three corners.
Capacity is stirred before anything is given. Plato: teaching does not put sight into blind eyes; it turns the soul toward the light.
“First thirst must be created, then the sweet and pleasant water given.” The psalmist is the one in whom the thirst is already awake.
All must “hold fast to the cord of wisdom”, since open teaching would cause uproar. The Gospel sends its messengers out as sheep among wolves, wise as serpents.
The reading advises against teaching openly. The same Gospel discourse tells the disciples to preach from the housetops what they heard in secret. Which counsel belongs to which circumstances?
No word is to be uttered “from which opposition to kings and the like might be scented”. Paul to the Christians of Rome: be subject to the higher powers.
The reading forbids words that might alarm rulers. The apostles, told by their rulers to stop teaching, said they must obey God rather than men. What may a teacher never agree to leave unsaid?
“If thou findest one receptive, turn to him; if thou findest one who turneth away, turn from him.” The Gospel’s instruction for a town that will not hear is to shake off its dust.

The reading tells the teacher to turn from one who turns away. The shepherd of the parable leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that is lost until he finds it. When is turning away respect, and when is it giving up?
“Make wisdom a lamp unto thyself and walk thereby in the darkness of the earth.” The psalmist’s lamp is the word of God.
The reading makes wisdom a lamp carried by the walker. The Buddha’s parting counsel has the same image and no other light: be lamps unto yourselves.
Those who come “claiming faith” are not to be trusted without “critical examination … and a long period of waiting”. The First Letter of John: believe not every spirit, but try them.

The reading counsels suspicion of certain newcomers. The Letter to the Hebrews counsels the opposite risk: welcome strangers, for some have entertained angels unawares. How does a community protect itself and remain open?
The precepts are “to tend the sick, raise the fallen, care for the poor and needy”. James calls this pure religion.
The purpose of religion is harmony, and it has been “clouded by the dust of vain imaginings”. Pascal says what it then becomes: people never do evil so cheerfully as from religious conviction.
The teacher “must also be utterly humble and lowly … and be totally self-effaced”. John the Baptist: he must increase, but I must decrease.
“Love thou the children of men and share in their sorrows.” Paul: weep with them that weep.
“To please the people is of the utmost difficulty. God Himself did not succeed in pleasing the people.” Paul gave up the attempt: if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
The reading sets aside the wish to please people. The same Paul says he became all things to all men, that he might win some. Where is the line between pleasing people and meeting them?
“May they consider themselves servants of humanity.” Jesus: whoever will be great among you shall be your minister, and the chiefest servant of all.
“Consider every poor one a prince … the poorer they are, the nearer they are.” James asks whether God has not chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith.

The reading sees a prince in every poor person. Proverbs records how the world sees him: hated even by his neighbour, while the rich have many friends. What does a community have to do for the reading’s sentence to be more than a sentiment?
After speaking, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá left gold and silver for the poor, so that words should not exceed deeds. Paul’s rule for giving: not grudgingly, for God loves a cheerful giver.
The reading admires a gift made tactfully to the poor. Thoreau distrusted the whole transaction and said he would run from a man coming to do him good. What makes help bearable to the one helped?
“What is needed today is the sanctification of hearts and breasts from rancor and hatred.” Lincoln asked a country at the end of a civil war for malice toward none and charity for all.

Blessed is one who reclines at ease “while his breast is illumined with the light of love for all the peoples of the world”. A character in Dostoevsky knows that love well, and how it thins as people come near. Is love for all peoples proved on the couch or in the room?
People are to be summoned “through goodly exhortations and gentle words”. Proverbs: a soft answer turns away wrath.
“It would be most regrettable should these precious times pass while one remains heedless.” The Letter to the Colossians: walk in wisdom, redeeming the time.
“Ideas and principles are helpless without a divine power to put them into effect.” Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Spend every breath in this Cause, and “inherit the heaped-up treasures of the realms above”. The Sermon on the Mount: lay up treasures in heaven, for where your treasure is, there will your heart be.
“Expend your every breath of life.” Saʿdī opens the Gulistān by counting what each breath already owes: two benefits, and thanks for each.
“Rest not for a moment, pause not for an instant.” Tennyson’s Ulysses: how dull it is to pause, to rust unburnished.
The reading allows no pause. Jesus, seeing his disciples with no leisure even to eat, told them to come apart and rest a while. What place has rest in a life of service?
“Gird up thy loins … Be swift in the path of God”; the charger is ready and the arena waits. The Letter to the Hebrews has the same contest: lay aside every weight and run the race.
“If thou be steadfast in this Cause … thou wilt find thyself assisted.” Joshua was promised the same: be strong, for the Lord is with thee.
“Send teachers to those parts”, and only such as are detached. Jesus sent seventy, two by two, and said the labourers were few.

The hope is that children “may be educated according to the teachings” and become lighted candles. Wordsworth thought children arrive already trailing light, and that growing up dims it. What does education add, and what must it take care not to put out?
“Give glad-tidings and joyful news to all Israel.” Isaiah: comfort ye, comfort ye my people.

“This is eternal sovereignty—to be imbued with the virtues” of God. Shelley’s king of kings wanted the other kind and left a boast in the sand. Why is the sovereignty the reading means not exposed to that ending?
A man who travels for commerce, the reading says, thinks only of his trade, “no matter what weather he encounters”. The merchant of the parable sells everything for one pearl.
“I hoped that after their graduation these boys will arise … but none of them fulfilled my desire.” Isaiah’s owner of the vineyard did everything for it and looked for fruit that did not come.
The reading records a teacher’s disappointment in those he educated. Ten were healed on the road, and one came back.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s joy is in women who “have been educated” and “raise such a call”. Proverbs praises the woman who opens her mouth with wisdom.
The reading rejoices in women who teach publicly. Paul’s instruction to Corinth was that women keep silence in the churches. On what grounds do the readings set that instruction aside?
“Make them … lamps of Thy guidance in that furthest shore.” Acts: witnesses unto the uttermost part of the earth.
“I complain not for myself … I sacrificed my spirit for Thy spirit.” Paul, in prison: to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
To a small child: now “is the time to jump about and to chant ‘O my God!’” The psalmist says that strength is ordained out of the mouths of babes.
“May your eyes be opened … and may your ears be unstopped.” The wording is Isaiah’s promise for the day of return.
“I have believed in Thee … and have arisen … to assist Thy Cause.” Isaiah, hearing the question “Whom shall I send?”, answered for himself.

corinthians-lest-i-be-a-castaway.text: But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway

philippians-preach-of-envy.text: Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds: But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice

james-swift-to-hear.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath

luke-count-the-cost.text: For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish

matthew-kingdoms-of-the-world.text: Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me. Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve

matthew-tombs-of-the-prophets.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! because ye build the tombs of the prophets, and garnish the sepulchres of the righteous, And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets. Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets

romans-zeal-not-according-to-knowledge.text: For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge

matthew-good-and-faithful-servant.text: And so he that had received five talents came and brought other five talents, saying, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents: behold, I have gained beside them five talents more. His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord

corinthians-not-with-enticing-words.text: And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God

john-speak-that-we-do-know.text: Verily, verily, I say unto thee, We speak that we do know, and testify that we have seen; and ye receive not our witness

psalm-lamp-unto-my-feet.text: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path

john-epistle-try-the-spirits.text: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world

romans-weep-with-them-that-weep.text: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep

mark-shall-be-your-minister.text: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many

james-poor-rich-in-faith.text: Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him

proverbs-poor-is-hated.text: The poor is hated even of his own neighbour: but the rich hath many friends

matthew-treasures-in-heaven.text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also

mark-rest-a-while.text: And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat

isaiah-comfort-ye.text: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned

philippians-to-live-is-christ.text: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain

psalm-babes-and-sucklings.text: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger

isaiah-eyes-of-the-blind.text: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped

analects-to-know-a-thing.text: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;-this is knowledge
analects-to-know-a-thing.author: Confucius
